extracted.intended_audience: reporters, cub reporters, copy editors and newspaper journalists
extracted.subtask_short: news writing sentence and word rules
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for writing clear, accurate, and interesting sentences and choosing precise, simple words in newspaper news stories. Covers grammar, pronoun/verb agreement, clause coordination/subordination, emphasis, brevity, diction, and common word misuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for the sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The same laws of accuracy and interest that govern the story apply to the sentence; because sentences are briefer and analyzable the rules are more rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even under deadline pressure the reader must not be able to tell how rushed the reporter was; sentences that are faulty, ungrammatical, or weak will lose readers. Strive for both accuracy and interest, with accuracy the greater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar (four principal violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good grammar is the first point of accuracy; main violations fall under four heads: faulty reference, incorrect verb forms, failure in coordinating/subordinating parts of a sentence, and poor ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City editors correct many grammatical errors; reporters should be familiar with and avoid these four classes of mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns referring to ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Every pronoun must refer to a particular word in the sentence and agree in gender and number; avoid using a pronoun to refer vaguely to a general idea not expressed by a particular word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear pronoun reference is a prolific source of obscurity in news writing (example: a pronoun 'which' used to refer to an idea rather than a specific noun).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of pronouns in number
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference words must agree in number with the nouns they refer to; watch collective nouns, distributive pronouns, and constructions with mixed singular/plural nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common errors occur after mob, crowd, everyone, anybody, and after two or more nouns. Examples illustrate wrong usage and the resulting obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pronouns with unclear antecedents buried elsewhere in the sentence so the pronoun appears to refer to an intervening word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This misuse is largely a clearness problem and is the most common error of faulty reference; illustrative examples show ludicrous results and how to fix them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split infinitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid placing an adverb between 'to' and its infinitive (e.g., 'to quickly run') as a general rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split infinitives are not always errors—use when precise meaning requires it—but as a rule reporters should avoid the construction; example shows awkwardness caused by bad placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitive and participle with verbs (tense relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinitives and participles have no finite tense of their own and express time relative to the main verb; misuse causes confusion about timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of relative time when using past infinitives or participles (example: 'had intended to have arrested' is misleading). Rewrite to express intended sequence clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangling participles
rubrics_metrics.description: A participle must have a definite noun or pronoun in the sentence to modify; otherwise the sentence implies the wrong agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions where the participle appears to modify an inanimate or unintended subject (example: 'Having arrived at the county jail, the door was forced open' is wrong). Provide corrected forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs must agree in number with their subjects; do not make the verb agree with the predicate or mix points of view for collective nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch qualifying phrases between subject and verb, correlative constructions (either...or, neither...nor), and the expletive 'there' (many writers err here). Choose singular or plural for collectives and be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor) only to connect words, phrases, or clauses of equal rank; do not use them to connect elements of unequal grammatical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faulty use (e.g., 'and who' connecting a participle and a relative clause) produces awkwardness and lack of clearness. Ensure elements joined by a conjunction are grammatically parallel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clauses unequal in thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not connect clauses that are grammatically equivalent but unequal in thought value with a coordinate conjunction; give the main idea independent clause status and subordinate lesser ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the primary idea in an independent clause and subordinate the lesser thought (examples show improved force when thought-value is respected). Beware overstrict observance that can make sentences ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipsis is omitting a word or phrase necessary to meaning; good ellipsis allows the omitted material to be readily supplied from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ellipsis is desirable for brevity but poor when the omitted words cannot be understood from context. Examples show good (Pope) and bad ellipses; omit words only when they can be precisely supplied by the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness in the sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: After correct grammar, clearness and force give a sentence its interest; clearness is more important—never write a sentence that must be read twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News stories are read rapidly; sentences should yield ideas with minimal effort. Examples show sentences that are clear only on a second reading and how to fix them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammatically connected phrases (proximity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep grammatically connected words, phrases, and clauses as close together as possible to preserve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misplaced modifiers or distant dependent phrases (e.g., 'over the governor's veto' placed far from the verb it modifies) cause reader confusion; rearrange to place modifiers adjacent to their heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlative conjunctions placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each correlative (either...or, neither...nor, whether...or, not only...but also) should come immediately before the word or phrase it modifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect placement changes meaning or makes sentences clumsy (example correcting 'Either the prisoner will be hanged or sentenced...' to place 'either' before 'hanged').

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of 'only' and 'alone'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Only' comes immediately before the word or phrase it modifies; 'alone' comes immediately after; neither should be placed between emphatic words or phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguity by placing these modifiers close to their targets (example shows incorrect placement of 'only'). Use 'alone' instead of 'only' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetic expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid long parenthetic expressions within a sentence; sentences within parentheses should generally be avoided in news articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two short, terse sentences are usually clearer and more effective than one long sentence containing doubtful parenthetic clauses. Example demonstrates rewriting into two sentences for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifted subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not shift subjects within a sentence without good reason; retaining the same subject in successive sentences aids clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting subjects weakens sentences; examples show how to rewrite sentences to keep the subject consistent and thereby improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence (sentence relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sentence must both convey its meaning and make clearer the meaning of preceding and succeeding sentences; phrases should follow in natural sequence and show their relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure connectives indicate the correct relation (example shows wrong 'but' where 'and' or nothing should be used). Check local logical relations as well as grammatical sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that appear to lack unity often lack proper coherence; improve unity by clarifying relations between clauses and making coherence explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences to make subordinate/main relations clear so that the sentence reads as a single, unified thought; example provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence emphasis (five methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gain emphasis by form, position, proportion, repetition, and delicacy of expression; put most important ideas in independent clauses and place them at the sentence's beginning or end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use position to place emphatic ideas first/last; transfer phrases from normal positions to attract attention; examples demonstrate improved emphasis by reordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion for emphasis (brevity and active verbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence emphasis varies inversely with length—brevity increases emphasis; reporters must condense and reduce predication to a minimum, using as few verbs as possible and preferring active verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense by removing unnecessary verbs/pronouns and reducing predication; 'as few verbs as possible and all verbs active' is cited as a newsroom slogan. Examples show how shorter sentences gain force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (use carefully)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition can provide coherence and emphasis but must be used sparingly; over-repetition often signals laziness and depletes sentence force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition deliberately for effect; avoid repeating the same adjective or phrase excessively (long example of 'beautiful' overuse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicacy is originality, cleverness, nimbleness, beauty of phrase, simplicity, restraint, tact—an intuitive quality that distinguishes experienced reporters from cubs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid beginning stories with fixed, hackneyed types of sentences; avoid affectation and indelicate personal allusions. Delicacy can be learned by practice though it cannot be simply taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of the sentence (accuracy and interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good sentence possesses two requisites: accuracy and interest; accuracy is the greater. Components of accuracy include grammatical correctness, definite pronoun antecedents, consistent verbs, correct ellipsis, clear relations among phrases, and correct coordination/subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reporter masters grammar, coordination/subordination, pronoun antecedents, verb agreement, ellipsis, clearness, brevity, and delicacy, his sentences will be accurate and interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words — accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, like sentences and stories, must be accurate and stimulating; accurate word choice comes first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always seek exact shades of meaning; search for the single noun, verb, adjective that best expresses the idea. Avoid looseness of thinking and inexact expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words — precision in word choice (avoid common misuses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select precise words—there is only one noun/verb/adjective to express a thought; avoid misusing words (e.g., 'lurid' misapplied) and be careful to distinguish similar words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides a long list of commonly confused or misused words and advises reporters to distinguish keenly between pairs (e.g., above/over, affect/effect, emigrate/immigrate). Never be content with 'very nearly'—search for the precise term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words — clearness through simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure interest, words must be clear, forceful, and simple; avoid technical, ornate, or big words and favor everyday Anglo-Saxon words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The average newspaper reader has a limited vocabulary; simple familiar words (home vs residence, begin vs commence, coffin vs casket) are usually most forceful. A list of high-register words with simpler alternatives is provided for guidance.
